paragraphs.text: VI. LETTERS OF LUCIFER AND OTHERS.
I. LETTER OF LUCIFER, PANCRATIUS AND HILARY TO BISHOP EUSEBIUS.
To the most honourable lord Bishop Eusebius, from Lucifer the bishop, Pancratius the presbyter, and Hilary.

Holy lord, now that the devil's head and his wicked promptings have been trampled underfoot, we ask you not to neglect the grace granted to you by our Lord. Please hasten, so that with you on the attack the doctrine of the Arians may be put to flight as soon as possible. For the Lord and his Christ know that, as the name of God was glorified at the coming of the most blessed apostles in the downfall of Simon, so at your coming, with Valens driven out, the scheming of the blaspheming Arians may be broken up and destroyed. Most holy lord, from the first day we came to Vercelli until today we have longed for your Reverence, and we pray the Lord that all the saints in this church may praise its lasting restoration and honour your spiritual strength with the praise it deserves. We believe this will come about, because we are confident that the passion of the Saviour cannot be overcome. May Christ the Lord keep you in glory, most holy and most blessed one.
II. LETTER OF POPE LIBERIUS TO LUCIFER, WHILE HE WAS IN EXILE.
Liberius the bishop to his most beloved brother Lucifer.

The enemy of the human race seems to have raged all the more fiercely against the members of the Church under the guise of peace. Yet your outstanding and singular faith, bishops most acceptable in the Lord, has both shown you approved by God here and already marked you out as martyrs for the glory to come. With what proclamation of praise, then, with what exultant voice can I set forth the merits of your courage? Placed as I am between grief at your absence and joy at your glory, I cannot find the words at all. I only know that I can offer you a more convincing comfort if you believe that I have been driven into exile together with you. Indeed, while I still hang in suspense, waiting, I am deeply saddened that a harsher necessity keeps me apart from your company for now. For I had wished, most devoted brothers, to be spent for all of you first, so that your love might gain an example of glory through me. But let this be the palm of your merits: that you were the first to come, through perseverance in the faith, to the illustrious glory of confession. I therefore beg you, beloved, to believe that I am present with you, to feel that in affection I am not absent, and to understand that I grieve greatly at being separated from your company for now. How great a glory you have won you can see best from this: those who were crowned in persecution could feel only the bloody swords of the persecutor, whereas you, soldiers of God devoted in all things, have also found false brothers to be your enemies and have carried off the victory over their treachery. The more their violence has been able to grow in this world, the greater the rewards of praise they are found to bring to holy bishops. So be secure in the heavenly promise, and since you have been brought nearer to God, lift me, your fellow bishop and a servant of God, up to the Lord by your prayers, so that we may bear patiently the assaults that keep coming, which inflict heavier wounds as they are reported from day to day, and that, with the faith unviolated and the state of the catholic Church kept safe, the Lord may deign to make me your equal. And since I wish to know more accurately what took place at the council itself, I beseech your Holiness to report everything faithfully in writing, so that both my mind, tormented by various rumours, and the strength of my body, which is already worn down, may feel the added support of your encouragement. [And in another hand:] May God keep you safe, my lord brothers.
III. LETTER OF FLORENTIUS TO LUCIFER.
Florentius to the most kind lord Lucifer.

Someone presented a book in your name to our lord and Augustus. He has ordered it to be delivered to your Holiness, and wishes to know whether this book was sent by you. You must therefore write down truthfully what the facts are, and send the book back so that it can be presented again to his Eternity.
IV. LETTER OF LUCIFER TO FLORENTIUS.
Lucifer the bishop to Florentius, Master of the Offices.

Your religious prudence, dearest son, was to be informed [?] by this letter of the following: the bearer of the book, who your Honour says approached the emperor in my name, was sent by my lowly self; and the book itself, as you deigned to request, was carefully examined and handed over to Bonosus, agent in rebus, to be delivered. It will now be for your nobility to defend without any hesitation what I have acknowledged. For when he begins to examine the reasons why I wrote in such a way, he will find us, by God's favour, standing glad against whatever is being prepared for our death.
V. LETTER OF ATHANASIUS TO LUCIFER.
To the most beloved lord, his brother Lucifer, bishop and confessor, Athanasius sends greeting in the Lord.

By God's favour we are in good bodily health, and we have now sent our dearest Eutyches the deacon, so that your religious Holiness may also deign to inform us of your own welfare and that of all your people, which is what we long and desire for. For we believe that through you confessors and true servants of God the state of the catholic Church is being renewed, and that what the heretics have tried to tear apart our Lord Jesus Christ is restoring whole through you. The forerunners of Antichrist have done everything they could, by the power of this world, to put out the lamp of truth; yet the Godhead, through your confession, has shown its light more brightly, so that their deceit can be hidden from no one. Before this they could still pretend; now they are called antichrists. For who does not detest them? Who does not flee their communion as a stain and the venom of a snake? Everywhere the whole Church mourns, every city groans, aged bishops suffer in exile, and the heretics pretend nothing is wrong; while they deny Christ, they have made themselves publicans, sitting in the churches and exacting taxes. O new breed of men, and new kind of persecution devised by the devil, that he should use such ministers for doing evil, and with such cruelty! Yet even though they do such things and have stretched their arrogance and blasphemies so far, your confession, religion and wisdom are no small comfort but the greatest solace and a great consolation to the brotherhood. For word has reached us that your Holiness has written to Constantius Augustus, and we marvel more and more that, though you live in the midst of scorpions, as it were, you still exercise freedom of spirit, so as to bring those in error to the light of truth by warning, teaching or correcting them. I therefore ask, and all the confessors with me ask too, that you deign to send us a copy, so that all may see the courage of your soul, and the confidence and freedom of your faith, not only from report but also from your writings. Those with me greet your Holiness; I greet all who are with you. May the Godhead always keep you safe, vigorous and mindful of us, most beloved lord and truly man of God.
VI. LETTER OF ATHANASIUS TO LUCIFER.
To the most glorious lord and justly most longed-for fellow bishop Lucifer, Athanasius sends greeting in the Lord.

I believe that news has reached your Holiness too of the persecution that the enemies of Christ, seeking our blood, have tried to wage even now against the brotherhood; yet our dearest friends can also tell your Reverence about it. They have dared to extend their fury through soldiers so far that they not only drove out the clergy of the city, but even went out into the deserts and laid their deadly hands on the monks. That is why I too withdrew farther away, so that those who had taken us in should not also suffer trouble from them. For whom will the Arians spare, who have not spared their own souls? And when can they turn back from their wicked deeds, as long as they persist in denying the Lord Christ, the only Son of God? This is the root of their depravity; on this sandy foundation they build their crooked ways, as we find written in the thirteenth Psalm: "The fool has said in his heart, 'There is no God,'" and soon after follows: "They are corrupt and have become abominable in their works." That is why the Jews, denying the Son of God, deserved to hear: "Woe, sinful nation, people full of iniquities, evil seed, lawless children." Why lawless? Because "you have forsaken the Lord." That is why the most blessed Paul, when he had begun not only to believe in the Son of God but also to preach his Godhead, wrote: "I am conscious of no evil in myself." So, following your confession, we too desire, holding fast to the apostolic tradition, to live according to the commands of the divine law, so that we may be found with you in that choir in which patriarchs, prophets, apostles and martyrs now rejoice. Although the Arian madness, together with an alien power, was so stirred up that, as long as they raged, the brothers were not even allowed to see the open air freely, yet in answer to your prayers and by God's favour I was able, though with toil and danger, to see the brother who usually sends both necessities and letters, from your Holiness and from others. So we have received the letters and books of your most religious and most wise soul, in which we have seen the image of the apostles, the confidence of the prophets, the teaching of truth, the doctrine of the true faith, the way to heaven, the glory of martyrdom, triumphs over the Arian heresy, the unimpaired tradition of our fathers, and the right rule of church order. O true Lucifer, who, as your name says, bearing the light of truth, have set it on a lampstand to shine for all! For who but the Arians does not see clearly from your teaching what the true faith is, and what the stain of the Arians is? Greatly and wonderfully, as light is separated from darkness, you have separated the truth from the cunning and hypocrisy of the heretics. You have defended the catholic Church, you have proved that the words of the Arians are nothing but fantasy, and you have taught that the devil's gnashings are to be trampled underfoot. How good and delightful are your exhortations to martyrdom! How greatly to be longed for you have shown death for Christ the Son of God to be! What love you have displayed for the world to come and for the heavenly life! You seem to be a true temple of the Saviour, who dwells in you and himself speaks these things through you, he who has given such grace to your words. You were loved by all before, but now so great a love of you is planted in everyone's hearts that they call you the Elijah of our times. Nor is that surprising: if those who are seen to please God are called sons of God, all the more fitting is it to call confessors, above all, sharers with the prophets. Believe me, Lucifer, you have not said these things alone; the Holy Spirit is with you. Where else does such a knowledge of the Scriptures come from, such a sound understanding of their meaning? Where such well-ordered speech? Where such exhortations to the heavenly way? Where such confidence against the devil and such proofs against the heretics, unless the Holy Spirit were dwelling in you? Rejoice, then, seeing clearly that you are already where your predecessors, now martyrs, are: in the choir of angels. We too rejoice to have you as an example of courage, patience and freedom. As for what you wrote about me, I blush to say anything, lest I seem a flatterer; but I know and believe that the Lord himself, who revealed all knowledge to your holy and religious soul, will repay you for this labour too with a reward in the kingdom of heaven. Since you are such a man, we ask you to intercede for us in your prayers to the Lord, that in his mercy he may now deign to look upon the catholic Church and rescue all his servants from the hands of the persecutors, so that all those too who fell through fear of the moment may at last lift themselves up and return to the way of righteousness, from which they have been led astray and now wander, wretched men, not knowing what pit they are in. For my own part I ask you especially to forgive me if I have said too little [?] in reply; my inexperience could scarcely draw what it could from so great a spring. And as for our brothers, if I was not able to see them as much as I wished, again I ask your forgiveness. Truth itself is my witness that I wished and longed to obtain this, and was so grieved that I could not; for tears have not ceased from my eyes nor groans from my heart, because we are not even allowed to see the brothers. [?] is also my witness that I have not been able to see even my own relatives since they began persecuting us. For what do the Arians not do? They watch the roads, they keep track [?] of those who set out and leave the city, they search ships, they patrol the deserts, they disturb houses, they harass the brothers, they contrive trouble for each one. But thanks be to God, the more they do these things, the more they are detested by all and recognised truly, as your Holiness has said, to be the slaves of Antichrist. And the wretches, though they are held in hatred, persist in their malice until they too are condemned by death, like their Pharaoh [?]. Those with me greet your Reverence; please greet those with you. May the divine grace of God keep you always safe, mindful of us, and blessed, truly [?] man of God, servant of Christ, sharer with the apostles, comfort of the brotherhood, teacher of truth, and most longed-for in all things.
VII. LETTER OF LIBERIUS.
Liberius the bishop to the most glorious Constantius Augustus.

Most serene emperor, I pray that your Clemency may lend me a kindly ear, so that I may open the purpose of my mind to your Gentleness. From a Christian emperor, the son of Constantine of holy memory, I would expect to obtain this without hesitation. Yet I realise that here I struggle, for in spite of repeated apologies I cannot win back to favour towards me your mind, which is ready to be appeased even towards the guilty. The address your Piety sent to the people some time ago wounds me deeply, though I must bear all things patiently; but that your mind, which is always given to gentleness and which, as it is written, never keeps its anger until the sun goes down, should keep up its indignation against me is a wonder to me. For, most religious emperor, I seek true peace with you: not a peace composed of words with deceit arranged inside, but one reasonably established on the precepts of the Gospels. It was not only the matter of Athanasius but many other things that had come into question, and for these I had begged your Gentleness that a council be held. That way, first of all, the cause of the faith, in which our first hope towards God lies and which the sincere devotion of your mind towards God especially desires, would have been carefully dealt with, and then the affairs of those who ought to admire our reverence towards God could have been settled. It would have been worthy of a worshipper of God, and worthy of your empire, which is ruled and increased by the piety of Christ, that your Clemency should grant us this especially, out of reverence for the holy religion to which you wisely give your attention.

But there are many who hasten to tear apart the members of the Church. They have invented the story that I suppressed letters, so that the crimes of the man they were said to have condemned would not become known to everyone: namely, the letters of the Eastern and Egyptian bishops, in which, in every one, the same charges against Athanasius were contained. But it is clear enough to everyone, and no one denies it, that we made the letters of the Easterners known, read them to the church, read them to the council, and moreover replied to the Easterners. We did not lend them our faith and our judgment, because at the same time the judgment of seventy-five Egyptian bishops concerning Athanasius stood against theirs, and we likewise read this out and made it known to the Italian bishops. Hence it seemed contrary to divine law, when the number of bishops on Athanasius' side was greater, to lend our consent to the other side in any respect at all. Theosebius, who had been sent and was hurrying to Africa, left these writings with us, if he keeps faith with God; and afterwards Vincent, who had been sent as a legate with the others, took all these writings to Arles, so that they would not be lacking, should a council perhaps be obtained.

Your Prudence therefore sees that nothing has entered my mind that it would be unworthy for those who serve God to think. God is my witness, and the whole Church with all its members is my witness, that out of faith in and fear of my God I trample, and have trampled, all worldly things underfoot, as the teaching of the Gospels and the apostles commands. I have done this not out of reckless frenzy but by the divine law, established and observed; and while I lived in another ecclesiastical ministry, I fulfilled nothing that belonged to the law out of boastfulness or desire for glory. And I came to this office, as my God is my witness, against my will. In it I wish to remain without offence to God as long as I am in this world, and I have always seen to it that not my own decrees but the apostolic ones were kept firm and guarded. Following the custom and order of our forebears, I have added nothing to the episcopate of the city of Rome and have allowed nothing to be taken from it; and preserving that faith which has come down through the succession of so many bishops, many of whom were martyrs, I desire always to keep it unimpaired. Now my concern for the Church and my very devotion persuade me to lay my case open to your Piety. The Easterners declare that they wish to be joined to our peace. What peace is this, most clement emperor, when among them are four bishops, Demophilus, Macedonius, Eudoxius and Martyrius, who eight years ago at Milan refused to condemn the heretical doctrine of Arius and walked out of the council in anger? Your fairness and clemency will be able to judge whether it is right to lend consent to their judgments, and what such consent would be and would amount to. What is now being attempted subtly, under the pretext of Athanasius' name, is nothing new. There still survive the letters that Bishop Alexander once sent to Sylvester of holy memory, in which he states that before Athanasius was ordained he had expelled from the Church eleven men, presbyters as well as deacons, because they followed the heresy of Arius. Some of these, now placed outside the catholic Church, are said to have found conventicles for themselves, and George in Alexandria is affirmed to be in communion with them by letter. What peace, then, can there be, most serene emperor, if bishops are summoned, as has now been done throughout Italy, and forced to obey the judgments of such men?

Hear something else, since your Serenity patiently allows it. There still survive the letters of the legates who had been sent to your Clemency, which arrived recently. In them they state that, because of the disturbance of all the churches, they had indeed earlier been willing to yield to the judgments of the Easterners, but had proposed a condition: if those same men condemned the heresy of Arius, they would on these terms be inclined to obey their judgments. This agreement, as they themselves state, is confirmed by written evidence. They go into the council; after deliberation the others reply that they cannot condemn the teaching of Arius, but that Athanasius, which was all they demanded, must be deprived of communion. From this let your Clemency consider this as well: whether the case of a man ought to be carefully and thoroughly examined only with the law of the catholic religion rightly preserved [?].

Therefore again and again I ask your Gentleness, your mind devoted to God, by the power of him who has shown all mortals how great he is in your defence, keeping before your eyes the benefits of him who rules your empire in all things: have these matters carefully dealt with, with full consideration, in an assembly of bishops. Then, with the times made peaceful through you by God's favour, and with your Serenity's consent, let everything be examined in such a way that whatever has been confirmed by the judgment of the bishops of God may be kept as a precedent for the future, once it is established that all have agreed to the exposition of the faith confirmed by so many bishops at Nicaea in the presence of your father of holy memory. So the Saviour himself, who looks down from above on the purpose of your mind, may rejoice, in so great a settlement of affairs, that you have rightly placed the cause of faith and peace even before the needs of the state. To entreat your Gentleness, then, that you may deign to hear our pleas with a kindly mind, it has been decided that my brother and fellow bishop, the holy man Lucifer, should set out together with my fellow presbyter Pancratius and the deacon Hilary. We believe that they will without difficulty obtain from your Clemency a council for the peace of all the catholic churches. May the clemency of almighty God keep you for us, most clement and most religious Augustus.
VIII. LETTER OF ATHANASIUS.
Athanasius, to those who pursue the solitary life and are strengthened in faith in God, his most beloved brothers in the Lord: greetings.

I give thanks to the Lord, who has granted you to believe in him, so that you too, with the saints, may have eternal life. But there are some who hold the views of Arius and go around the monasteries for no other reason than to lead the simple astray, passing themselves off as people coming to you and returning from us. There are others who insist that they do not hold the views of Arius, yet they go and pray together with those people. So, since our most sincere brothers urged me that it was necessary, I have taken care to write to you. I want you to keep the godly faith that the grace of God works in us, sincerely and without deceit, and not to give the brothers any occasion of stumbling. For when someone sees you, who are faithful in Christ, in communion with such people or praying together with them, he will surely think that it makes no difference, and so he falls into the mire of impiety. So that nothing of this kind may happen, dearest brothers, make it your concern to turn away those who hold the views of the Arian impiety, and to avoid those who are thought not to hold the views of Arius but who pray with the impious. Above all, it is right to shun communion with those whose opinions we abhor. So if anyone comes to you and, as blessed John says, brings sound doctrine, say "greetings" to him and receive such a person as a brother. But if someone pretends to confess the right faith, yet is clearly in communion with those people, urge him to give up that habit. If he promises to do so, treat him too as a brother. But if he persists in a contentious spirit, avoid him as well. I could indeed have made this letter much longer, setting out from the divine Scriptures the pattern of this kind of teaching. But since you are wise and anticipate those who write to you, and since you are especially devoted to self-discipline and are fit to teach others as well, I have dictated this briefly, as one in earnest writing to those in earnest. I am confident that by living this way you will preserve a pure and sincere faith, and that those people, once they see that you do not pray together with them, will be helped by it, since they will fear that they may be counted as impious and as sharing the views of the impious.
